extracted.intended_audience: Anyone who desires to better understand the history and core principles of Administrative Law; especially first- and second-year law students
extracted.subtask_description: A multi-module online course introducing the history, doctrines, institutions, and controversies of the U.S. administrative state, aimed at building foundational understanding (first-year difficulty). Covers rulemaking, executive and congressional oversight, and judicial deference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand the history and function of the administrative state
rubrics_metrics.description: A deep dive into the history and function of the administrative state - and exploration of questions over the scope of power that agencies frequently exercise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Course promises both historical and analytical looks at the growth of the administrative state; experts 'offer answers but also ask the viewer to ponder new questions.' Emphasis on understanding why the administrative state exists and how it operates over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain whether agencies were anticipated in the Constitution and their place among the three branches
rubrics_metrics.description: Were agencies anticipated in the Constitution? Where do they fit into the structure of the 3 branches of government?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This unit provides a brief overview of administrative law, the various types of agencies, and the growth of the modern administrative state — i.e., students should be able to situate agencies constitutionally and institutionally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify types of agencies and the growth of the modern administrative state
rubrics_metrics.description: Provides an overview of administrative law, the various types of agencies, and the growth of the modern administrative state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Know the different forms agencies take (independent commissions, executive agencies, etc.) and the historical expansion of regulatory government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand the scope of agencies' authority to write regulations
rubrics_metrics.description: The scope of agencies' authority to write regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes the substantive question of how much lawmaking power agencies possess compared to Congress, and contextual facts such as the volume of the Code of Federal Regulations relative to statutes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain core processes of agency rulemaking, including notice-and-comment
rubrics_metrics.description: Core processes of agency rulemaking (notice and comment rulemaking).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Students should understand procedural steps agencies follow to promulgate rules, with specific attention to notice-and-comment as a central process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess accountability, review, and scrutiny of administrative rules
rubrics_metrics.description: The review and scrutiny that rules are subject to, and how agency rulemaking fits in with the democratic process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Covers mechanisms for public and judicial review, standards of review, transparency, and how rulemaking integrates with democratic accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate tradeoffs between agency expertise and congressional legislating
rubrics_metrics.description: What are tradeoffs for relying on agency expertise instead of Congressional legislating?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Students should be able to weigh benefits of technical expertise and speed against concerns about democratic legitimacy and separation of powers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain how the executive branch and presidential control affect agencies, including OIRA oversight
rubrics_metrics.description: How does 'who the President is' affect administrative agencies? How does the Office of Internal and Regulatory Affairs (OIRA) oversee these agencies for the Executive branch?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes understanding appointment/removal powers, political control via agency heads, OIRA's role and limitations (e.g., which agencies are reviewable by OIRA and why), and whether OIRA serves both the President and the public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand Congress's role in lawmaking and oversight of agencies
rubrics_metrics.description: Who makes laws? Congress has power from Article I to create laws, yet the vast majority of laws today come from administrative agencies. How does Congress oversee agencies? Do they exercise meaningful checks on agency power?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze whether administrative law undermines enumerated powers, evaluate congressional oversight tools, and consider possible reforms to increase congressional control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain judicial deference doctrines and the courts' relationship to agencies
rubrics_metrics.description: When and how do Courts defer to an agency's interpretation of its own statute? (Chevron doctrine; other forms of deference such as Auer, Skidmore). What does the Administrative Procedure Act say about whether courts should defer to agencies? What is the relationship between administrative agencies and Article III judges? Are administrative law judges (ALJs) constitutional?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand Chevron's standard, alternatives (Auer, Skidmore), statutory constraints from the APA, separation-of-powers concerns, and contemporary debates about the constitutionality and role of ALJs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engage critically with normative debates about administrative power
rubrics_metrics.description: Some topics will aim to challenge the assumptions many hold about the administrative state, encouraging the viewer to think more critically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The course frames questions like 'who watches the watchmen?' and presents a range of perspectives; learners should be able to assess arguments for and against expansive administrative authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be prepared for first-year difficulty material delivered in short video modules
rubrics_metrics.description: Total run time: 2h 22m; Total videos: 45; Difficulty: First Year. Watch short, digestible videos on a range of key topics. Videos can be watched in each Module’s website, on Youtube, or delivered to you in your email inbox!
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical expectations: no academic credit, material is free, suitable as a supplement to classroom learning; learners should be ready for concise modules rather than full-semester depth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge viewpoint diversity and speaker ownership of opinions
rubrics_metrics.description: Our speakers have a range of perspectives and expertise that they bring to bear on the topics presented. All views presented belong to the speakers, and don’t represent any kind of 'official' view.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using course material as evidence or citation, treat individual presentations as perspective-driven commentary rather than institutional pronouncements.
